title: Sequenced request affinity and tail mitigation labbook
content:
Summary:

This labbook documents an exploratory series of experiments probing the effect of request sequencing / affinity heuristics on continuous-batching scheduler behaviour, with the explicit goal of reducing 99.9th tail latency for mixed-length workloads without sacrificing overall throughput.

Motivation and high-level idea:

We observed intermittent 99.9p spikes in production traces where long-context requests arriving shortly after many short requests caused batch-formation churn and KV-cache pressure, leading to heavy tail amplification. Hypothesis: if the scheduler preserves a light-weight notion of 'sequenced affinity' that groups requests likely to share kernel-hot paths or KV cache regions, we can lower expensive context switches inside a batch and reduce variance in GPU kernel execution times. Secondary hypothesis: lightweight per-origin slotting (affinity tokens) can avoid starving fairness-critical clients while still preserving batching efficiency.

Goals:
- Measure impact of sequencing/affinity heuristics on p50/p90/p99/p99.9 latency and throughput.
- Understand interaction with timeouts and max-batch-size under continuous batching.
- Surface fairness regressions across tenant/service classes when affinity is enabled.
- Identify failure modes and resource-pressure thresholds where affinity harms more than helps.

Environment:
- Runtime: local staging cluster (3 x A100-40GB) running the continuous-batcher branch with lightweight tracing enabled.
- Model: open-gpt-2-13B-quant (representative, has non-linear kernel cost vs. seq length).
- Traffic harness: synthetic mixer (bursty Poisson), two tenant classes: interactive (short avg tokens=40, high QPS), background (long avg tokens=800, low QPS). We overlay microbursts to emulate PLG burst patterns.
- Measurement windows: 30-minute steady-state runs after a 10-minute warmup.
- Key metrics: p50/p90/p99/p99.9 latency, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, KV cache miss rate, fairness index (ratio of median latencies across clients), drop/retry counts.

Config matrix tested (representative subset):

1) baseline-continuous: default continuous-batcher (flush-timeout=8ms, max-batch=64), no affinity.
2) affinity-soft: sequencing affinity enabled, soft grouping token TTL=120ms, affinity-prefill=true, flush-timeout=8ms, max-batch=64.
3) affinity-hard-slot: same as affinity-soft but with per-origin slot reservation (2 active slots per origin), flush-timeout=8ms, max-batch=64.
4) affinity-shortbias: affinity with bias toward grouping short requests together (short-first insertion), flush-timeout=4ms, max-batch=64.
5) timeout-sweep: baseline with flush-timeouts=[4ms,8ms,16ms] to observe interplay.

Notes on affinity implementation (lightweight):
- Each request carries an optional affinity-token (derived from client-id + recent kernel hotkey) assigned at ingress for this experiment.
- Token TTL is ms-level; the scheduler keeps small token->slot maps and prefers to add matching tokens to existing batches unless that would exceed per-batch length-diversity heuristics.
- Implementation avoids strong head-of-line blocking by allowing token-preemption when batch timeouts approach.

Key findings (summary):

1) p99.9 reductions for mixed workloads: affinity-soft reduced p99.9 by ~18–26% versus baseline in 30min runs where background long requests were interleaved randomly. The biggest wins occurred during microbursts where short requests preceded a long request within <200ms window.

2) Throughput and GPU utilization: throughput (tokens/sec) remained within ±3% of baseline for affinity-soft. affinity-hard-slot showed ~6% throughput drop in high contention runs due to slots being held but delivered better tail stability.

3) Batch composition effects: affinity increased same-token-hotpath coalescence: fraction of batches with homogeneous-length > 2 increased by 22%. Kernel time variance across batches decreased (measured using tracer-derived kernel-duration histograms), correlating with lower tail.

4) KV cache interaction: affinity reduced reclaims in many runs (KV miss rate down ~7%) because grouped long-context requests tended to reuse similar KV segments. However, in affinity-hard-slot runs with many low-cardinality tokens, KV pressure rose slightly due to slot-holding increasing live set diversity on GPUs.

5) Fairness: affinity-soft maintained fairness index within 1.1x of baseline. affinity-hard-slot improved tail fairness for tenants with stable tokens but penalized ephemeral clients (e.g., webhooks) who couldn't get slots.

6) Timeout tradeoffs: shorter flush-timeouts (4ms) amplified preemption and reduced affinity's benefit; 8ms was a good sweet spot in our harness. Longer timeouts (16ms) increased p50 but sometimes further reduced p99.9 when workload burstiness was low.

Representative run table (30-min):

- baseline-continuous: p50 18ms, p90 36ms, p99 120ms, p99.9 420ms, tokens/sec 1.00x, gpumiss-rate 0.12
- affinity-soft: p50 19ms, p90 34ms, p99 110ms, p99.9 320ms, tokens/sec 0.98x, gpumiss-rate 0.11
- affinity-hard-slot: p50 21ms, p90 38ms, p99 115ms, p99.9 290ms, tokens/sec 0.94x, gpumiss-rate 0.13
- affinity-shortbias: p50 16ms, p90 30ms, p99 130ms, p99.9 460ms, tokens/sec 1.02x, gpumiss-rate 0.10

Interpretation and interesting failure modes:

- Token cardinality matters: when affinity-token cardinality was low (many clients reuse same token), affinity-hard-slot helped; when cardinality was high (ephemeral tokens per request), it effectively serialized work and harmed throughput.

- Short-bias heuristic (grouping shorts first) reduced median latency but sometimes increased tail because when a long request arrived late it blocked a slot whose batch already contained many short items, forcing a larger kernel to run and increasing completion variance.

- Slot holding + KV working set growth: slot reservations kept batch membership stable but increased the live KV working set on GPU; under memory pressure this led to small regressions in max memory and occasional OOM kill in stress tests. This suggests any slot mechanism needs to be memory-aware and possibly have eviction-backed slot reclamation.

Operational notes (tracing and instrumentation):

- Traces used: trace-ids run at tf: 2024-11-06T10:12:00Z trace root = T-8427; microtrace correlation token: mt-17d3.
- Important logs: scheduler.log rotated per experiment. Use flags --trace-batcher --kv-metrics to reproduce captured histograms.
- Dashboard: experiment dashboard at confluence://serving-runtime/affinity-experiments (linked above).

Next steps / experiments to run:

1) Cardinality sweep: systematically vary token cardinality and client churn to identify tipping point where affinity becomes harmful.
2) Memory-aware slots: add a slot eviction policy that considers current KV working-set and test under memory-constrained GPUs.
3) Adaptive TTL: have token TTL auto-adjust by measuring batch-stability signals rather than fixed ms TTL.
4) Hybrid heuristics: combine affinity with early KV prefetch hints (from request metadata) to further reduce miss rates.

Open questions / unresolved items:

- What is the production-safe default? affinity-soft looks promising, but we need a noisy-gate rollout plan and a rollback strategy if token cardinality spikes.
- How to expose knobs to tenants so they can request affinity hints without enabling total slot reservation? API surface design pending.
- Interaction with canary rollouts: affinity changes can hide fairness regressions; need canary-specific fairness probes.

Todos (short):
- [ ] Create ENG ticket for cardinality sweep and add to perf sprint (Amit)
- [ ] Prototype slot-eviction by KV-pressure (Nora)
- [ ] Add per-client fairness dashboards to dev console (Liam)
- [ ] Patch README for affinity feature flagging + rollout notes (Maya)

Raw artifacts and links:
- Kernel histograms: s3://redwood-experiments/affinity/kernels/2024-11-06/*.json
- Run logs: /tmp/affinity-run-20241106.tar.gz (staging host)
- Traces: trace root id T-8427 (see tracing UI)

Quick verdict (internal):

Affinity-based sequencing is a promising lever for tail reduction in workloads with meaningful kernel hotpaths and moderate token reuse. The simplest "soft" affinity (best-effort grouping, TTL ~120ms) gives most benefits with limited throughput impact and looks like a candidate for an opt-in canary. Hard slot reservation needs more safeguards (memory-aware eviction, cardinality detection) before broader rollout.

Notes to reviewer:
- This is exploratory; numbers vary with harness design. Please reproduce with your workload and add notes to the confluence dashboard.
- If you need traces/plots not included here ping me in #eng-serving-runtime and I will export.
